extracted.intended_audience: members of the public or prospective clients trying to understand legal professional titles and how to verify an attorney's credentials
extracted.subtask_description: Explain the meanings and practical implications of the labels J.D., Esq., lawyer, attorney, and related honorifics in the United States, and how to verify whether someone is authorized to practice law.

rubrics_metrics.name: J.D. (Juris Doctor)
rubrics_metrics.description: "J.D." stands for Juris Doctor — also known as a law degree. Similar to other academic suffixes like "Ph.D." or "M.D.," a J.D. indicates that the titleholder has completed law school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a J.D. from an accredited law school entitles that person to apply for and take any state's bar exam, but it does not allow them to practice law before being admitted to the bar. Persons who graduate with a J.D. but do not take or fail the bar exam are not members of the bar and are not authorized to give legal advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM (Master of Laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced law degrees are called "LLMs" (master of laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a J.D., LLM denotes an advanced legal education but does not necessarily indicate the person is able to practice law or represent clients; LLM is an additional academic credential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esquire (Esq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Esquire" (or its abbreviation, “Esq.”) is not any kind of official title. Esquire is an honorary title that is placed after a practicing lawyer's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing lawyers (those who have passed a state's or D.C.'s bar exam and have been licensed) commonly use "Esq." on signs, letterheads, business cards, signature lines, and sometimes on official court documents. However, the requirement to include a state bar number on filings can make the suffix largely irrelevant. Historically, "Esquire" referred to helpers of knights—this origin has little bearing on modern practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney vs. Lawyer (equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney and lawyer mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only people who are licensed to practice law should advertise themselves as either an attorney or lawyer. The distinction between solicitors and barristers in England does not apply in the U.S.; in the U.S., after obtaining a license in a jurisdiction, a lawyer/attorney may appear in that state's courts on a client's behalf (subject to occasional additional court-specific admissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar admission / License to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing a state's bar exam and being licensed by that jurisdiction's bar association is what authorizes someone to practice law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A J.D. alone does not confer authority to practice. To determine whether an attorney is licensed and able to represent clients, look them up on your state's bar association website; if they are listed as able to represent clients, they are authorized, and if not, they may have a J.D. but cannot provide legal advice or represent you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-specific admissions (e.g., federal courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some practice areas or courts require additional admission to appear before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, bankruptcy is conducted in federal court, so bankruptcy lawyers must obtain the extra step of being licensed to appear in federal courts before representing clients there. Obtaining such additional admissions does not change an attorney's title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify attorney via state bar number
rubrics_metrics.description: Every attorney should be able to provide a state bar number that you can use to verify their license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bar number to confirm licensure status and review any records of unethical behavior or malpractice. Do not rely solely on seeing "Esq." or the word "Attorney" after a name when choosing legal representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to address an attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not need to address an attorney by any specific honorific in correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is customary and acceptable to use Mr./Mrs./Ms. Smith in correspondence rather than starting an email "Dear Attorney Smith." Use the attorney's personal preference when known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles vs. substance when hiring
rubrics_metrics.description: There's little to distinguish between the names that lawyers call themselves; titles are not a reliable indicator of competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing which lawyer to hire, the attorney's title (Esq., attorney, counselor-at-law, etc.) should not be a major consideration; focus instead on qualifications, licensure, experience, and ethical record. Some titles (e.g., "counselor-at-law") may be used to highlight a lawyer's advisory role, but this is a matter of preference and presentation rather than a formal difference.
